newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE - Foreigners to shake up Indian insurance.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Foreigners to shake up Indian insurance.

text.p: India is expected to announce new steps to open up its lucrative insurance sector to foreign investors when Finance Minister P. Chidambaram presents his budget this week.

Spurred by growing international clamour and the need to speed free-market reforms launched in 1991, India has taken several steps to lure investment in insurance, but has stopped just short of actually letting foreigners in.
Following pressure from the United States and the World Trade Organisation, India has established a regulatory mechanism to open up the industry, currently dominated by two state-run firms.

Chidambaram is widely exected to seek parliamentary approval to formally set up the insurance watchdog when he presents his budget for fiscal 1997-98 (April/March). The budget is provisionally set for Friday (Feb 28th).

Foreign investors -- 22 firms from Germany, Switzerland, Japan, the U.S. and Britain have already queued up -- will get a chance to get their feet wet. Marine insurance is among the areas analysts expect Chidambaram to throw open.

"The Finance Minister has assured (us) that he will make a statement along with his budget about the sequencing of the events he wants in the industry," N.I. Rangachary, the chairman of the Insurance Regulatory Authority (IRA), said recently.
SECTOR GROWING 11 PERCENT A YEAR
The Finance Ministry estimates the insurance sector is growing at the rate of about 11 percent annually.
The Life Insurance Corp of India (LIC) and its younger sibling, the General Insurance Corp (GIC), have ruled the sector since it was nationalised in 1956.
By 1996, LIC officials say, new business had grown to 520 billion rupees ($14.5 billion) a year, compared with 3.28 billion rupees in 1957.
Critics say LIC has become increasingly insensitive to its customers while enjoying this stupendous growth.
Many consumer activists say LIC, which provides coverage for about 110 million of India's 930 million population, is wedded to inefficient ways.

"In case of a dispute, it takes a minimum of six years and a maximum of 18 years before that weeping widow, aged parent, or minor child -- who in the process becomes a major -- gets the claim," said Manubhai Shah, of the Consumer Education and Research Centre.
INDIAN GOVERNMENT USED LIC AS A MILCH COW
In the pre-reform era, the Indian government made use of the vast funds at the LIC's command to intervene in the stockmarkets or direct the country's economy in other ways, Shah said.

"It looked upon LIC as a milch cow, controlling its funds for the mobilisation of financial resources to be invested in national economic or industrial development programmes, regardless of the needs of the insuring public," he added.
As a result, Shah said, Indian insurance products are skewed towards encouraging long-term savings, as opposed to term insurance, which pays off only in the case of death.

"The LIC has registered a growth of 19 percent over the gross premium income for 1994/95 which aggregates 131.49 billion rupees," said F.K. Daruwalla of the Bombay-based MF Reinsurance, in an analysis of the industry's performance in 1995/96.
"As a percentage of GDP, this represents just one percent," Daruwalla said. "Thus the potential for developing the market is immense in both the life and non-life sectors."
LIC AND GIC MUST RESTRUCTURE TO FIGHT CHALLENGES
Analysts say that unless LIC and GIC restructure and revitalise to fight off the challenge from newcomers, aggressive new entrants will lock them out of the potential growth ahead.
LIC officials agree with some of the criticisms levelled against the firm but stress that they are continually launching new products to help mop up funds.
"Generally the perception has been that LIC has not been able to cater to the different needs of customers in terms of its products," said managing director G. Krishnamurthy.
"Services have not been as efficient as we would like them to be."

But the LIC has grown more than 14 percent in terms of new policies over the 10 months of the fiscal year 1996/97 (April/March) to January 31, compared to the same period the previous year, said G.N. Bajpai, LIC's north zone manager.

"We have tried to deal with the problems not just of people dying suddenly, but also with the problem if they live too long," Bajpai said, explaining why LIC's most popular insurance products are long-term savings instruments.
"We have tailored the products to the Indian psyche, which is still not prepared to forfeit the entire premium if the death does not occur within the term," he added.
Both giant twins LIC and GIC have suffered from a degree of shortsightedness in the past, analysts say.
POTENTIAL FOR STATE-RUN FIRMS TO EXPAND
"There are many areas the two firms could have expanded into," said John Steele, of the British insurance major Commercial Union Plc, which has tied up with India's K.K. Birla group.

"There is no reason why the GIC could not be the biggest reinsurer in this part of the world -- the Middle East, Africa, and so on," he added. "It has all the qualifications, and an excellent track record."

For Chidambaram's reforms to succeed, his government, a fractious coalition of 14 parties ranging from free traders to communists, has to carry along policy opponents who fear foreign insurance firms would transfer large funds out of India.
"I am ready to commit that we will bring in one billion rupees each for life and general insurance," said Steele.
India requires foreign firms to bring in one billion rupees of paid-up capital each for life and general insurance licenses.
Government critics fear that aggressive foreign firms will take away business from LIC and GIC, but LIC has no such fears.
"There is enough opportunity for everybody," Krishnamurthy said. "There is vast potential with so many working people. Our growth rates may slow, but we will introduce new products."

Steele agreed. "It's not a question of new entrants taking a slice of the pie, but the pie actually grows bigger as well," he said. "A liberalised insurance sector will see a flowering of insurance products." ($ = 35.86 Indian Rupees)
